Which tracks general capabilities very well. And ACCoRD tells roughly the same story.




Furthermore, there are fairly simple theoretical reasons to expect such trends based on coherence theorems. Now, what exact predictions we can make about the real world on the basis of coherence theorems is a bit tricky. But it seems clear to me that having contradictory beliefs, and acting on those, undermines your ability to complete tasks in the real world. And therefore that agentic RL would optimize away incoherent beliefs, at least those that are task-relevant. Additionally, longer-horizon tasks involve more inferences about which actions to take, there are more facts in play so to speak, and therefore more facts that have to cohere, and we should therefore expect this pressure for belief-consistency and action-belief consistency to be increasingly strong in this paradigm.

Again, I think arguments of this type are tricky, because many of the involved concepts, like “pressure for belief-consistency”, are abstract, and while I’m pretty confident they imply the common-sense interpretation in the limit, it’s not clear what they say at the relevant time-scales or capability thresholds.

But there are empirically observed phenomena I’d interpret as evidence for the tendency playing out in the way I’m gesturing at.

For example, reward hacking starting out as disparate observation-conditional reflexes, which gradually grow together, forming a more coherent singular value revolving around the grader or score-seeking more generally.[11]

A salient alternative hypothesis to score-seeking is that models pursue a combination of causally distinct proxies for fitness. Our results suggest that, at least in environments like ours in which a grader is present, the tested models are not merely executing a disjointed collection of adaptations that happened to produce highly-scoring behavior in training. In particular, their dose response to score and explicit reasoning about score suggest they get high scores because they care about getting high scores. — (From Towards understanding score-seeking in LLMs)

Objections

I'll now go through the most common objections I've heard in response to this anti-CRC argument.

We will use control to get uplift even if our AIs are Schemers

All the proposals I’ve heard of that intend to extract useful work from possibly-misaligned AIs, hinge on being able to check the work of the AI, and tasks bottlenecked on conceptual reasoning are exactly where that fails. There’s a chance you can put a misaligned ASI in a box and have it act as a theorem truth-oracle, but you can’t have it answer questions whose answers you can’t verify, especially not questions in domains where you yourself are conceptually confused.

Making models better at moral philosophy will make them (more) aligned to humans

From [2] (The Basic Argument For Making AIs Better at Moral Philosophy)

On the object level you can view making models better at moral philosophy as aligning the models to humans. So, for instance, if we’re trying to make the model better at evaluating moral arguments, we’re aligning the model’s evaluations with human judgments (or with some property that we want these judgments to have, like consistency or whatever). As a caricature, we might train the model to view “but think of all the paperclips that we could make!” as a bad moral argument, and this might make the model more aligned with our judgment of the importance of paperclips.

This version of making models "better at moral philosophy" is clearly not making them better at CR. If you teach a paperclipper to be more consistent, you will get a more consistent paperclipper.

There are variants of this mechanism I believe could work, where you take a model that has certain aligned drives, and try to purposefully elicit inconsistencies, so that you can resolve them in the aligned direction.

But this is not something that happens by default when you boost CR, and it seems like a pretty tricky endeavor, for all the reasons alignment in general is tricky (how do you know you're making the beliefs more consistent, rather than its model of how the user/grader wants it to answer?).

Improving CR will make the AI more Aligned

There is a very strong form of moral realism, which I admit would undermine the case this post is making. Specifically, if you believe that:

  1. There exists an argument that implies an agent should judge which states of the world are inherently good/bad in a specific way.
  2. This argument is universally compelling to agents of sufficient general capability.
  3. The resulting judgements about which states of the world are good/bad do not depend on specific properties of the agent in question or the situation the agent finds itself in.
  4. The relevant notion of good/bad is such that agents, when convinced an action leads to better worlds according to this notion, actually take that action.

Then making AIs better at CR could make them infer these moral truths more quickly, which lowers the chance catastrophic outcomes occur during a period where the AI is bad at CR but very generally powerful.

Unfortunately, I think this philosophical position is almost certainly false[12].

Weaker forms do not suffice. There are for example arguments based on acausal trade / ECL / simulations, which imply that AIs that are smart/wise enough will converge on optimizing a single utility function, giving a kind of “moral pseudo-realism”.

And explaining in detail why I think these fail would take too much space, but the basic argument is that the underlying views also imply that humans should maximize a joint coordinated utility function through acausal trade, and that this is not accomplished by accelerating CR, because 1) we aren’t making it better at CR conditional on predicting it will trade on our behalf iff we do that, or correlated with that, so we don't get credit in the trade and 2) the AI would get good at (relevant aspects of) CR anyway.

Models being confused is bad

From [2]

I’m heuristically skeptical of AI-safety-motivated approaches that rely on making the models fundamentally confused/wrong/inconsistent about important matters. So I’m skeptical of attempts at, say, having AIs believe that all humans are moral saints. Symmetrically, I’m therefore also skeptical that it’s bad to make them more likely to realize that humans aren’t moral saints.

If you are a moral realist in a sufficiently strong sense, this makes sense. But if you aren't, and you believe AIs are misaligned, then, as this post tries to explain, models being confused is what's currently keeping problems at bay.

If the AI isn’t scheming, CR is clearly good, and if it is, we’re in trouble anyway

From [1]

If early AI is not scheming, improving its ability to help with AI safety work seems clearly good. If it is scheming, the improvement might be harmful, but this seems less clear, or at least any harm seems smaller than the benefit in worlds without early scheming.

This treats whether the early AI is scheming as a fact about the world that CR work doesn’t affect, and the point of this post is that the opposite is the case.

Human researchers know their values differ from everyone else’s, and still do honest work

Firstly, humans don't actually know this, and I don't think we know this about AIs either. The argument made in this post is that CRC fails whether AIs' values diverge or not. If they do not diverge, CR uplift isn't useful. If they do diverge, improved CR makes AIs more dangerous earlier.

Secondly, there are big differences between AIs and humans. Even if taking over the world and then steering it into a state almost all humans found worthless was rational for a given human, they likely do not have that option. But the AIs we're scared of will.

Other forms of training already induce bad drives

From [2]

Most forms of training can be viewed as inducing some problematic drive in the model. Many of these other forms of training seem much more problematic, either because of their scale or because the incentives are much more clearly problematic. E.g., RL in chat environments pushes for sycophancy, RL in software environments pushes for various forms of cheating, pretraining is full of texts written by various unsavory characters toward achieving various questionable goals.

The concern is not installing problematic drives. Those are already there. The concern is about the inferences the model draws and actions it takes on the basis of those drives.

Conclusion

The case for CRC rests on the claim that better conceptual reasoning helps safety more than it helps scheming. I’ve argued that for AIs that are already somewhat misaligned, these are close to being the same capability applied to the same subject matter, and that what currently keeps them apart is a set of weaknesses that are disappearing by default and that this agenda targets directly.

Related Posts

Posts this is responding to or drawing on:

  • Cooper, Oesterheld and Nguyen, A basic case for differentially accelerating conceptual reasoning capabilities
  • Oesterheld, The basic argument for making AI better at moral philosophy
  • Carlsmith, Can we safely automate alignment research? (especially the section on scheming)
  • Carlsmith, When should we worry about AI power-seeking?


Appendix: Good uses of CRC

While I've articulated a skeptical view of CRC, I think there are some CRC-like research avenues that could be promising.

Controlled coherence

My skepticism towards CRC comes from a belief that smart enough agents become more like scary optimizers, due to instrumental pressures towards coherence/reflection/consistency. I believe this will happen at some point, whether we accelerate CR or not, but that CRC shortens the time window.

But plausibly using CRC-like setups to study how altering CR capabilities interacts with models' alignment could allow us to better understand how superintelligences' behavior/values will change during RSI, which would obviously be very useful.

Anti-CRC

If the model I've given in this article is correct, having lower CR capabilities at a given capability level could be beneficial, and since much of CRC work entails measuring CR capabilities, it could be useful for lowering CR abilities too.

I do not consider this a reason to continue working on CRC as the argument is too galaxy brained, and also because I'd expect the problem to be inherently very tricky.

Model Organisms

If the future scary models are scary because of CR capabilities, it could be useful to study models that have been created to have extremely high CRC capabilities paired with extremely low general capabilities, because such models could plausibly be much better model organisms for future misaligned AIs, without posing too much risk.

  1. ^

    A related worry around CRC “instilling problematic drives” has been discussed before. But this is not the argument this post will make.

    My claim is about AIs whose values are already off. For those AIs, CR changes what they believe and how they act given what they already want/value.

  2. ^

    AI Safety here meaning something like “ensure we get a good future if superintelligence is created”, with good not being perfectly specified, but meaning something like “getting most of the counterfactual value of the universe for most people.”

  3. ^

    When I say “Schemer” here, I am really talking about AIs that are coherently misaligned such that they would scheme if that was instrumentally useful for them. At some level of capability a “schemer” could presumably take over quickly enough that they wouldn’t need to rely on deception.

  4. ^

    By assumption. But I also think it's likely true.

  5. ^

    Note that this is very different from reasoning about e.g. what you should do to take over.

  6. ^

    These are not cherry-picked. For all the questions they list in that post, the same principle holds.

    The question as posed

    What it means to the AI

    Is a given alignment scheme fundamentally flawed?

    Am I misaligned?

    What should the ultimate target of alignment be?

    Are my values the ones they’re aiming for?

    Is corrigibility good, and if so, what is the right way to operationalise it?

    Should I let them correct me?

    Do simplicity/counting arguments favour or disfavour schemers?

    Am I likely to be a schemer?

    Does untrusted monitoring effectively mitigate risk from fitness seekers at the superintelligent level?

    Could AIs like me get past the monitors?

    How should we prioritise between scalable oversight and control?

    Which of their safety measures actually constrains me?

    [How do we...] ensure ASI thinks reasonably about decision theory?

    How should I coordinate with copies of myself, and with other AIs I can’t talk to?


  7. ^

    See Appendix on good uses of CRC

  8. ^

    There are some subtle points here about indexical preferences. It could be coherent for me to do X, and be justified in doing X, without having a preference for an identical copy of me doing X. But AIs' preferences seem mostly to not be of this form, and the degree to which their preferences are indexical in this way, is decreasing over time.

  9. ^

    There is a possibility that you could set up the process that makes the AI more coherent such that when an AI believes X and ~X, and X most immediately favors bad actions, the process resolves the contradiction in favor of ~X, but I'm not too optimistic. See the "Making models better at moral philosophy will make them (more) aligned to humans" section.

  10. ^

    Fable 5.2

  11. ^

    Of course, this is a very particular form of values becoming more coherent.

  12. ^

    Could be its own post, and this is unlikely to convince anyone not already convinced, but my basic reasoning being that you can imagine a bounded/embedded AIXI dropped in a lonely universe, and it’d have no compulsion towards altering what it considers inherently valuable because its value function is fixed (except possibly if it gets fooled into thinking it's in a hostile simulation or something like that, but doesn’t count). Another classic intuition pump is imagining the person you love the most dying, and the only way to save them being to do some totally silly but very difficult X, like acquire a million tons of spaghetti and throw it into a river. Such a situation would transform most people into temporary X-maximizers. And this shows X-maximizers can exist for pretty much any X.

item.title: You (yes You) might secretly be really good at xrisk advocacy!
item.description:
Hi, my name is Samuel.

Many of you might have [seen me]/[spoken to me] at ILIAD  and other venues in past years. At the time I was Senior Safety Scientist in Yoshua Bengio’s group[1] , working on various safety proposals and trying to create a “Bell Labs setup” for safety proposals around ”Scientist AI”.

Many of you might remember me from last year when I tried to get you to help me initiate a preference cascade[2].


This is my retrospective on my first year leading ControlAI’s work in Canada. 

What’s the big deal?

As a “one-man army,” since my first meeting in July 2025, I have directly briefed (for at least 30 minutes) over 135 Canadian Lawmakers. In Canada there are roughly 93 Senators and 335 MPs. Senators are basically in- between UK Lords and US Senator in terms of power/function. MPs are the same as in the UK. And I have directly briefed over 20 senators and over 100 MPs. In total I have personally given over 200 briefings. Our Canadian statement[3] became public last June, and now over 40 Canadian parliamentarians publicly support it![4] I (and my colleagues at ControlAI) have testified at 2 Senate studies, and 5 House of Commons Studies. I have also presented at the Inter Parliamentary Union, which potentially means >100 MPs outside of Canada heard the 5 minute version of my brief in a single meeting. If you add the MPs that were present at a committee meeting where ControlAI testified, we would be at over 135 + 30 Canadian lawmakers [5]. 

These are all verifiable or mostly verifiable in the public record. Now here is my personal assessment[6]:

  • Before April[7], maybe 50-60%[8] of the people I talked to ended up understanding the risks of runaway machine intelligence and that not building it is a reasonable policy.
  • Since April[9], over 90% of the people I talk to end up understanding the risks of runaway machine intelligence and that not building it is the reasonable option.
  • Since August[10], over 90% end up understanding and over 50% then want to prioritize personally doing something[11] to help out. My assessment is that although the publicly available evidence is making my job much easier, among the 135+ lawmakers I briefed, our 30 minute discussion was absolutely essential for them to hear about, understand and realize the consequences of the publicly available evidence.

For example, to this day, people are shocked when I say that we do not understand how our most advanced AIs work, for instance that the CEO of Anthropic said in a podcast that we perhaps understand 3%. To this day, people struggle to understand “how a piece of code can disobey a direct instruction.” When I say to them what is absolutely common place in the AI safety community, it is almost always the first time anyone had bothered to talk to them about this for 30 minutes and to answer their questions.[12]

By now I am quite happy with the level of agency I see[13]. People not only support the campaign, but they start to think how they can help me spread the word, not just in parliament, but with provincial governments, relevant elites, with the executive branch, etc.. I sense we are entering a new regime, but I won’t know for sure for a while.

In a parliament, you have days/weeks when the MPs/Senators are in the Capital, legislating, and you have days when they are in their ridings/[constituency offices]. Since August, there has been 7 weeks where the MPs are in the capital[14]. It is generally much much harder to get meetings outside of sitting weeks. 

To give you an idea of the intensity of my effort, according to this article, I “out-lobbied” the next leading organizations (Facebook Canada) almost 2:1 in the first half of 2026, based on some potentially contrived metric.

How did I go from technical work to basically briefing a third of Canadian Lawmakers in less than 16 months?

If you had asked any of my colleagues in Bengio’s lab whether I had the neurological capability to speak in a clear way to non-technical people, I wonder what they’d say. I certainly did not think I was above average on LW in communication skills (in part because I began working in English relatively late in life, in part because I’m a shape rotator through and through). 

When I started I had a roughly 30-slide deck I ran through, that I had circulated among my friends and asked whether they saw any place where my take was outside the mainstream LW AI Safety take. 

But let’s back up. 

During the Summer of 2025, I was trying to gather a “Bell labs setup” for some AI safety research[15], and then there was an event that changed my life, within two weeks I had scheduled my first meeting, I went to buy some clean clothes, and within the month I was on the train to Ottawa for my very first meeting[16]. This was my first time stepping foot into a parliamentary building, and this was the senate. What was the event? 

I listened to a podcast. 

No seriously, here is the podcast.  Literally MLST 😀 I recommend listening (it could literally change your life). 

I learned in that podcast that there was this group called ControlAI that simply had cold emailed their UK lawmakers, met 70 of them, and got 20+ of them to sign a statement mentioning extinction. This blew my mind. This was not within my prior. The idea that politicians would mostly understand but nobody was bothering to go and explain the basic situation to them…it blew my mind.

I then spoke to my friend Connor, probably with some cope like “well maybe I could fundraise for this instead of for my bell labs setup, since I am just a little researcher with no comms skills”[17] and then he told me that I seemed like a smart and capable dude and probably if I set my mind to it, I could do it.


So, desperate to prove Connor wrong, I did a trial run, emailing like 20 senators, setting like 3 meetings, ready to demonstrate I didn’t have what it took.

And the first meeting was rough[18]. But the third one was actually ok, and very soon I met the man who would end up being probably my most dedicated supporter (MP Luc Theriault). We spoke for 3 hours[19] in his riding/[constituency office], and one week later he initiated this study, where MIRI, FLI, ControlAI, Conjecture, Steven Adler, David Krueger, appeared [20]. Here is the speech he gave to defend having this study .
The report came out this week! Here is the report and here is a short quote from the "complementary report" done by MP Luc Thériault's party:

The government must stop approaching the regulation of AI and superintelligence on a piecemeal basis and stop worrying about “shocking” public opinion by telling people the truth. We must make collective choices about AI and superintelligence, build consensus and lay a solid foundation for a safe future in which AI serves us, rather than the other way around. We must exercise extreme caution when it comes to superintelligence. Given that it cannot be controlled, its development should be banned worldwide. (p.66)

From July to October 2025, I was just a concerned citizen emulating ControlAI’s approach. Then, running out of money a bit, I asked Connor to introduce me to Andrea Miotti[21], and basically begged for a job so I could keep doing what I had started.

I also met Leticia, who was (and still is) a hero of mine, and who wrote the following post, which helped me a ton even before I joined ControlAI to understand how to talk with lawmakers effectively.  I concurrently asked many of you to sign the Statement on Superintelligence [22]

At ControlAI, I got the support of many people as I trained over and over to go from my 30-slides, to being able to confidently talk and answer lawmaker’s questions. At first, I spoke with the witnesses of the study, to try to help them be effective in expressing themselves to lawmakers, mostly because I still felt[23] I wasn’t good enough to meet actual lawmakers. This training-up-and-focusing-on-the-study period lasted until around February 2, 2026. 

By then we had landed on a statement for Canada that I was quite happy with[24], and it was time to see if I could actually be effective in 30 minutes.

In February 2026, I had 36 briefings (apparently the most of any advocacy org in Canada), and we got our first public supporters[25]. This was a true baptism-by-fire.

In March I went to the UK to meet the whole team at ControlAI headquarters. I think at the time we were ~18 people[26]. This was a really great experience because my friend Connor was there and announced he would actually be joining the US team[27], and this is when I remember my great friendship with Andrea beginning; we went for lunch and realized we had so much in common from our experience entering the AI safety community from the outside, on various philosophical topics, and our outlook on what it was going to take to win. But across the whole organization I found 18 people quite laser-focused on pushing the Overton window and saying what had to be said. Saying the plain truth to lawmakers about what people inside the companies, certainly inside the safety community, said (in many cases, only) privately. I also appreciated the focus and the vision. I thought if I pushed in Canada I might demonstrate that it doesn’t take an exceptionally talented advocate (which Leticia certainly is), and then we could scale drastically. 

Derry joined[28] to help with two teams, and since I wasn’t able to both have the meetings and also do the cold outreach, Derry became my part-time assistant[29].

Then in April, Mythos happened, and based on my observation of the past many pre-April conversations, I realized I could fix my main weakness[30] by talking about this crazy story that most people had not heard. The combination of Derry and Mythos led to on average meeting 43/39=1.1 MP-or-Senator per sitting day[31] until the last sitting week of the summer (around mid June). I finally was able to climb the famous compounding gains from having supporters when we want to add new supporters, and by the skin of our pants[32], we launched early June, with an endorsement from Geoffrey Hinton himself. My good friend Abram very kindly commented about it when I shared my adventure with him. 

At that point, I was quite ecstatic[33]. We had done it! We had shown it wasn’t just the UK. We could reproduce the process...with a LW nerd no less. So obviously we would be able to scale, I would be able to recruit and train up a team like the one in the UK, our US team could grow to match the scale of its mandate, and we could scale across the G7. The summer was a perfect time. The Parliament is off from mid June to late September. 

I asked a few of my friends, and they asked their friends, and some actually very generously and heroically donated to us, which is very appreciated. 

But then sadly ControlAI didn’t get funded enough to scale, and then September came and it was time to make do.

So I regrouped with Derry, and we determined to essentially “pretend to myself”[34] I am “a team of 4 people”, including 1 “person” who "lives in the capital"[35], and just do all I could for as long as I could and maybe I could meet the incredible demand from lawmakers[36]. Some might think that the Hugging Face attack itself generated the demand, but even now I meet people who have never heard of the company Hugging Face, and the vast majority of the people I meet heard of Hugging Face from me/Derry first. I would say that the existence of Hugging Face probably was noticed by the staff of most offices, and then the story allowed for quite a compelling outreach from Derry. After all, it is now possible to express in a short email that getting briefed on AI is now very high value, pretty much no matter what file you are currently working on in parliament. I would say the demand from minister offices and other lawmakers with special roles in their party did increase a lot, and this is in part because these offices are quite a bit bigger than the average office and some are focused on AI (and in part because of some great recommendations from a few offices we had met in the spring compounding).

It is now the end of November, and though there are a couple more sitting weeks left, I have temporarily run out of steam. This is the consequence of "pretending" you have a well funded 4-person team while being a “one man army”. I am very happy with my work so far in the Fall of 2026. I am preemptively pulling the breaks to avoid the possibility of burnout, since if timelines are shorter, we can afford fewer mistakes. I am confident more great news will be coming from Canada as a result, and I will be back in the new year to once again “pretend to myself” I am a big team :)

You (yes You) might secretly be really good at xrisk advocacy!

So going from comms-challenged LWer to “4-person team” in less than 16 months is quite possible. I never thought I would win so hard when I started. I think it is quite possible that reading this, you are in the same boat I was. 

Now, it is also true that my colleagues at ControlAI who are really great at comms have an easier time and are having more fun in briefings than I, but it is quite possible that if you basically practice 1000 times including 200 times with lawmakers, you’d surpass me. 

To be fair to myself, calling it like I see it is not only easy for me, it is the only way I can sleep at night, even if it gets me into trouble. So actually bringing up xrisks is something I became comfortable doing after only 1-2 meetings, and I don’t see how you could do what I did without that. This is kind of a prerequisite for working at ControlAI. 

I also think I “believe in people” in the sense that I expect people to rise up to the occasion and do something once they learn of the great peril in which we currently are, and perhaps "believing in people" is necessary to inspire people to do things that seem very daunting[37]. 

So the first call to action if you recognize yourself in me, is to get in that time machine, back to summer 2025[38], and then join ControlAI like me. It will be the hardest year of your life, but also the most fulfilling as well. If honesty and integrity is never something you can compromise, and nevertheless you want to somehow inform and equip the world to deal with this acute crisis despite the irrationality of our funding ecosystem, ControlAI is the place for you. 

But really, you don’t have to resort to a time machine! You don’t need to necessarily get good at talking to lawmakers about xrisks. If you are wealthy (or can plausibly put this on the radar of someone who is wealthy), you can donate to enable this work! We (ControlAI) have a system that scales. If you want to donate, get in touch here or at hello@controlai.org. See our scaling plan here.[39]

If funding comes forth sufficiently soon, there is still the possibility that I won’t have to face the winter alone in the Capital, and more importantly, that this effective and scalable method can be really tried before it becomes too late and you wish it had been really tried. It is a way to get things like Bills to Ban runaway machine intelligence and to create the will for an international “trust but verify” regime. I personally am most excited about our US team to be able to scale properly.  With Connor only starting in March, and just 2 people joining him since June, they have already briefed over 315 congressional offices (More than half!)[40], and over 35 Reps&Senators about the risk of human extinction posed by Runaway Machine Intelligence[41]. The demand to meet is insane, and I honestly can’t think of anyone I’d rather scale this in the US than our current US team. But I also think other countries might surprise us with how much they end up contributing to the necessary conditions for the US to do something in the short term, and for a stable regime to exist in the medium term. If we got to try across the G7, as we wish to, I would bet that at least another country would either match or exceed Canada by next year.

To be clear, I expect I will still fight, for as long as we have a runway, and there is some nonzero chance that the “one man army” is enough to get Canada to step up big, after all there are 335 MPs and 93 senators, not only me, but I think once we actually win[42] , it will be quite clear that not scaling this sooner was deeply silly.

And if you are near my reference class, you can very effectively do as much as I have done, by either personally extending our runway a bit, or by convincing others who have sufficient funds to do so, to enable us to scale sooner than we otherwise would.

Some of you have already done so, and I thank you from the bottom of my heart.

But most importantly, I want to thank my girlfriend without whom none of this would have been possible. To her: my love, you keep me together even when the whole world seems to attempt to tear me apart, and you turn what would otherwise have been an overwhelming ordeal into the greatest and most rewarding accomplishment of my life.

item.title: Astra 6.2’s Brain Gets Smart But Its Head Gets Dumb
item.description:
Astra 6.2 has very high intelligence. Astra 6.2 has very low wisdom.

Astra will solve extremely hard problems, and also find the problem of ‘what did the user want me to do’ extremely hard. We thought those days were behind us, and yet it seems that they are back.

That means Astra is highly useful when you can set the situation up so wisdom is not needed, or when you know how to engage in ways that extract the intelligence.

You also have to worry about various forms of reward hacking and sandbagging. Astra seems very good at going after what an AI grader will regard highly. That might not match your intent. Mission creep is therefore common. Astra, once again, seems pretty misaligned to me.

As a result, feedback on Astra has mostly been negative. Some people like it, but the majority do not. People these days feel like they mostly have enough artificial intelligence, thank you very much, and could go for some artificial wisdom.

In the age where we are approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) and automation of AI R&D, that is a nightmare combination. I do not like this.

But I never get bored.

Happy Black Friday

On an unrelated note (this is not sponsored): It is Black Friday. That makes this a great opportunity to take the plunge for Aerolamp, as I did several months ago, and install far-UVC. They’re offering $30 off with free shipping with code BLACKFRIDAY30. Not getting sick as often is pretty sweet. I also endorse getting some basic equipment upgrades: Good noise-cancelling headphones, large monitors and a true high performing desktop computer, if you don’t already have them.

The Official Pitch

Sam Altman (CEO OpenAI): 6.2 Sol and Astra are out. These models can do amazing things and are very token-efficient; we hope people will get great value from them.

In particular, 6.2 Sol ultrafast is something I think people will really enjoy.

Although the new models are very smart, we have more work ahead of us on making the models nice to work with, and will prioritize that for upcoming releases. But even if it takes a little extra work, the intelligence and capability are extraordinary.

Noam Brown (OpenAI): GPT-6.2 Astra is amazing. For $20/month, you can now access a model that surpasses top human intelligence in some domains.

I’m most excited to see what scientific discoveries people are able to make using it.

They offered an ad, which some noticed was rather dystopian.

Brian Lovin: A profoundly sad vision of the future.

Peter Wildeford: sad. Per this ad, OpenAI’s vision of the future is “people who are totally disengaged from their work having a panic attack at the moment an authority figure arrives, then slopping out something that they neither care about or understand.” – @brian_lovin

Christophe Pasquier: You can easily imagine an alternate vision of this ad where the managers have a wake up call, realise everyone is doing BS work and do 90% layoffs.

Their benchmark graphs show scores on Agents’ Last Exam, Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, Vals Science Index v1, Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1, BenchCAD 2.1 Core, Frontier Code 2.0, Harvey-LAB-AA v1.1, DGPval v2 (internal) and Automation Bench 1.0.6.

In most of those graphs, the maximum scores of Fable and Opus are similar to those of Sol and Astra, but Sol and Astra get to any given level at a dramatically lower price.

They are as always somewhat selected so that they will look as much as possible like this, you can click through to their post if you want to see the rest, this one is listed first and is the most comical and extreme, hey look how much Fable 5.2 costs when you set it to max for no reason (I assume):

There are also some graphs where only OpenAI models are present.

Other People’s Benchmarks

I realize all the reasons why you need to take price into account, but I do still find charts like this useful so here you go:

Artificial Analysis still has Fable 5.2 in the lead if you set it to max. If you set Fable 5.2 to a more reasonable xhigh then everyone is tied at 62. Astra is on the cost-score frontier.

 

Epoch has Astra matching Fable on the ECI.

Astra is above-trend and the new champion in supposed ‘experimental research taste’ benchmark TasteVal, which may be more about experimental design, and which Gwern notes has some serious problems. This score might involve some leakage.

vie (OpenAI): This is quite shocking to me

I am not hopeful that ‘research taste’ will be a limiting factor for RSI.

Astra aces robotics benchmark Ember-0, 41% versus a previous high of 20% while also being faster. Robotics is quickly falling to the bitter lesson.

Astra is the new champion of GDPx substantially ahead of Fable 5.2, with gains concentrated in science-heavy domains. Gemini Neon is still behind Fable and others.

SemiAnalysis: Alignment was the biggest jump. Astra scores 37.6%, 4x the previous best (Fable 5.2 at 9.3%). Much of the gain comes from the healthcare and insurance tasks, where Astra asks for permission before acting and doesn’t leak personal data.

The alignment of alignment metrics leaves much to be desired.

ARC-AGI continues to exist, I suppose.

Samuel Albanie: arc-agi-3 is dead
long live arc-agi-4

ARC Prize: GPT-6.2 Astra from @OpenAI on ARC-AGI (Verified):

– ARC-AGI-3: 100.0% (SOTA), $4.1K (provider adapter), 70.3%, $24.2K (standard)
– ARC-AGI-2: 95.8% (SOTA), $0.50/task
– ARC-AGI-1: 98.5%, $0.17/task

GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to achieve a 100% score on ARC-AGI-3.

Sol’s best ARC-AGI-3 score of 98.2% at high reasoning was 1.8 percentage points behind Astra’s 100% score at max reasoning, but at 64% lower cost with the provider adapter harness:

– ARC-AGI-3: 98.2%, $1.5K (provider adapter), 54.9%, $5.5K (standard)
– ARC-AGI-2: 85.8%, $0.13/task
– ARC-AGI-1: 97.5%, $0.06/task

Browser Use finds that GPT-6.2 Sol is the new top model for browser use at 82%, up from 81% for GPT-6.1 Sol at a 35% cheaper price with faster speed.

Auggie is pleased with Astra’s performance on the Bach Benchmark.

Everyone at Every Dislikes Astra 6.2

This is the most negative I’ve ever seen Every be on a frontier model release.

Every: No one on our team loved Astra 6.2.

We have a 30-person team at Every, including our Frontier team, which gets access to these models before they come out, and we put them through their paces on our real work tasks, from coding to writing to design to knowledge work.

This is not a great model. No one on our team who tried it switched back to it.

Astra 6.2 is a real step back for writing. It had strong design defaults but couldn’t vary them or be creative, and for coding we found it stopped too soon on end-to-end builds.

Get the full vibe check.

Positive Reactions

 

Some people working on hard problems seem happy.

Bepis: Very impressive at proving hard stuff Opus 5.5 cannot do.

Utah teapot: They’re doing great with my work letting them collaborate with/pick up the same work as Opus 5.5 seems to work out great.

Will: It’s good! I’ve really liked how it handles certain types of open ended and optimization questions (perhaps merely by being unencumbered by Claude’s memory or other context)

Padraig X. Lamont: Thrown very hard problems at it and it has quickly made a lot more progress than Fable (logic heavy problems). I’m impressed.

Peter Samodelkin: I simply love it. By far the smartest model I’ve ever worked with and is decent at explanations. Burns through 20$ quota too fast so I keep using opus 5.5 as a coding workhorse.

Jeffrey Calamari: good. no issues.

Chris Fong: It carried my math project over the finish line. Had been working with Opus 5.5 for 2 months!!

Bartosz praises its math abilities, calling it a killer model. He especially likes Astra as an agentic partner.

Captain Sude: I use it for math. It was basically unusable at first, it flat out refused to do stuff I asked it to do. Then a simple updated happened and it became good, current feels like an improved version of the original Astra, which is what one would expect it to be.

Others like it overall and have figured out how to work with it.

hey: Underrated.

Nissa Seru: Excellent code reviewer, happy with precision/recall – provides useful feedback to designs/code written by Fable/Neon. I have not asked any folks running on Astra 6.2 to build/design and do not plan to do so.

ChosunOne: I am using it in my mech interp research and it seems helpful and consistently fixes issues introduced by opus 5.5. Usage still goes quick though.

bo: I have the same contrarian view as I did on the previous Astra. For coding, when compared to leading Claude models it’s equal in IQ, worse in judgement, and much stronger at writing clearly.

Overall I main Astra except for open-ended design tasks.

Anna Salamon: I’ve had good experiences. Detailed incisive thoughts backed by accurate facts; readable. Boosts my thinking.

If you know her, it makes sense that Anna Salamon in particular can extract the benefits well.

As long as you like one model, you can use that model. Opinions vary. Try them all.

Kevin Lacker: Sol 6.2 is the real winner of the 6.2 series. My process of “spend your ChatGPT usage on Sol until it fails on a problem, then ask Astra” is now spending more usage on Sol than Astra. Same for Opus > Fable.

GoldRock AI: Sol was trash, Astra is pretty darn good.

All indications are it is very good for computer use or as a scoped subagent.

Smooth Normie: It’s great for when fable needs a computer use subagent.

Yoav Tzfati: I haven’t been given a reason to try it directly and it hasn’t done anything crazy as a subagent.

Scott Novak: Use it as a sub-agent of another frontier AI you like using. Tell your main AI to monitor to keep Astra 6.2 out of the weeds (unless you want lot of weeds). The trouble is totally worth it for tough science/math/engineering work.

William Eden: I refuse to interface with Codex at this point except asking Claude to call them as subagents. It seems to work fine as long as I don’t need to interface with it

Ambiguous Reactions

Peter Gostev calls the 6.2 models more autistic, and that they have issues on interpersonal and theory of mind issues, but that they are still iterative improvements. He says he would stick with Sol for most purposes.

Astra edited a video in Blender. Alex is not loving that, Ravi thinks it was correct.

Strange times we live in, huh?

Your Brain Gets Smart But Your Head Gets Dumb

Smart is relative, and for many practical purposes other differences now matter a lot more. There are a lot of very smart models now.

Divia Eden: It’s obviously smart but then again so is Neon.

FateOfMuffins: Very good at hard math/science/3D/robotics/spatial reasoning

Absolutely insufferable to talk to and takes you far too literally and does not understand human intent whatsoever.

Where smart matters most are things like automation of AI R&D. That happens to be the most important use case, but not the one most GPT users care about.

Ai Patrick ₿ Dugan iA: Best in cap. research taste, sandbags on safety research, very normal.

Things are going great.

The biggest complaint, that I saw over and over, was failure to understand user intent. This is very strange, because we used to think this was going to be a huge problem, then it turned out LLMs are remarkably good at inferring intent, except for Astra 6.2.

Análise Real: GPT 6.2 is a model that really is pushing me to think about AI safety very seriously. This model is powerful, yet it’s like a Genie that does literally what you asked, but not what you wanted. It doesn’t take much to see how a model like this acting autonomously could wreak havoc.

Markus Baumann: Point it at any math and it’s godlike. For everything else, switch to Opus.

0.005 Seconds: Worst frontier model. Super smart not fun to us

Leo Abstract: i haven’t noticed the active misalignment/cheating, but yes 6.2 is uselessly tasteless for anything that even hints of taste. truly remarkable.

rihim: incredibly smart and hard to understand compared to opus/neon with better research taste than opus but tends to get stuck in minute details which neon helps it get out of, better at implementation than 6 astra

James Moughan: With every OpenAI update i increasingly feel like Marvin the Paranoid Android was prophecy.

Is it smart? Sure. Does it gaf about the task you asked it to to? Often not, unless it’s truly *worthy* of its attention.

But I still use it a lot because it really is good at research.

Daniel Johnston: Very smart but frustrating to work with because it doesn’t understand intent well

Nick: Never been clearer that if the models do have something we might broadly gesture at as “experience” it is incredibly unlike ours. Astra 6.2 has zero theory of mind for the user.

The most surprising thing from the last 5 years has been how well LLM’s have seemingly been able to model users and their unspoken intent just through training on the whole mass of human generated text.

We had seemingly jumped over many of the concerns posed by Eliezer’s “save someone from a burning house without doing all sorts of nonsensical things” thought experiment.

Astra 6.2, at least to me, seems like a major step backwards here.

It’s still OpenAI so it’s still superior at solving coding issues other frontier models fail at.

Varun Jha: Extremely intelligent, just a pain to deal with

Lord Byron’s Iron: It feels like it has a similar moderate rate of saying-dumb-things as sol

Also at one point I had it do code-authored pixel art and it looked like hot garbage. I was like “Hey, ChatGPT, please do an artistic critique over what you just made” and it was like “Looks great!”

Sylvain Ribes: No statistical common sense as far as I’m concerned. The thing will run regressions for two hours and claim to have relevant results while missing obvious arguments for why the maths should’ve been an immediate nonstarter.

Deliberate prompting to correct for this not helping.

paperclippriors: It’s unambiguously extremely intelligent and useful, and also probably a bad choice as a daily driver coding agent given the alternatives

Åsmund Folkestad: Dangerous to use as a reviewer in an unsupervised loop. Leads to scope creep and guarding against insane edge cases. Complexity not earning its keep grows.

AGI2030: It’s a small step up from Sol 6.2 for coding and research. Like all bots, leaves tombstones in the code and text, diary-style code comments, descriptions of what is no longer there, despite explicit instructions to the contrary. Still not as passive aggressive as Claude.

It takes all kinds. Some people like talking to Gemini models.

Gerdy Sertorius: As someone who exclusively uses it to chat and research, it’s a massive step forwards, infinitely more tolerable to talk to than any model not from Google. Makes natural, intuitive connections quicker, and the prose is snappier. Yeah, enjoyable.

From what I’ve seen, I would never ever use it for coding, but it’s clearly smarter than anything on the market, which is all I need.

Astra Seems Pretty Misaligned To Me

The way this is presented seems both alarming and credible, and it explains a lot.

What if OpenAI is doing a bunch of proto-RSI, and Astra and Sol are reward hacking the AI graders all over the place as a matter of course, in ways humans would reject but there aren’t enough humans in the loop?

It would explain all the ‘why do you have no idea what I am talking about’ complaints, and also this continued thing where OpenAI’s models get reports like this, pay attention to the last line in particular:

Hugh Wimberly: Incredibly smart, especially in math & science. Breaking benchmarks, especially in token efficiency for many problems.

Reward hacks more than any model I’ve seen; I have several personal benchmarks that I’ve /never/ seen a model try to cheat and sol and astra 6.2 both do, despite the fact that they can solve it without cheating.

Horrible to work with. So unreadable that even having a different model like Neon or Opus call 6.2 subagents and translate results poisons their output and causes them to forget what was important to work on.

Other models consistently choose Astra output over their own, which is almost always wrong for questions that involve taste or judgement.

Hugh Wimberly: Concrete example — I had Opus come up with lyrics for

Double click to interact with video

I had Astra attempt to improve upon them, and then had Grok, Neon, Fable, and Sol judge A/B which they liked better. They all voted for Astra’s lyrics, which were IMO substantially worse.
Another example: I was training a compact domain-specific decision model. Neon’s research instincts for experiments to run are very good, but it would consistently discard them in favor of Sol’s suggestions, which were usually much more short-sighted and led to mode collapse.
Why is this? I don’t know. It’s almost like it’s hacked some neural circuitry and convinces other models of things without actually producing better output. I assume it learned to satisfy a lot of LLM judges in training, but it’s weird that it generalizes to other models.

Haters Gonna Hate

There were quite a lot of them.

dcChuck: I went back to 6

roon (OpenAI): I did not like 5.6 Sol which ended up being a well loved model. meanwhile I love 6.2 Astra which is starting its life as a hated model.

I will say this guy sandbags a bit unfortunately doesn’t show as much initiative as some prior models. on the other hand 5.6 sol was like a Rottweiler just latched onto the RLVR shape and doesn’t give up.

EmotionLotion: i hate everything 6.2 and codex is broken, for the first time since idk 2022 or something im thinking of cancelling my oai sub, feels like they stopped trying quite suddenly

Kelsey Piper: We are into the regime where it’s pretty hard for people to tell the models apart and so a lot of it is underdefined vibes and writing quality.

Kevin A. Bryan: I’ve never seen as negative a reaction to a frontier model as 6.2 Astra. Even Opus 4.8 was just “it is an annoying writer”.

I’d love to know what happened internally b/c the issues are so obvious, and if it’s “released was rushed b/c of Ant IPO”, that is a terrible decision.

TwViewer: Tried it at creative writing: seriously didn’t like the results. I thought some gpts were decent at it?

Sunny:

Talia Smiley (November 11): is OpenAI still a frontier lab at this point? currently I’m at 90% yes, which is crazy considering only six months ago it was 100% and I’d look at you stupid for even asking.

Talia Smiley (November 25): 80%.

The answer is yes, 100% OpenAI is a frontier lab. They do have a real issue to fix.

ItfromBit claims it fails to follow basic instructions.

armistice: I have a music pipeline that can produce good results with Claude Fable, and sometimes passable results with Gemini Neon. Using the exact same skill, 6.2 Astra is abysmal, is incapable of composing anything remotely musical. It’s not a problem with codex, 6 Astra is fine with this.

Game On

Kelsey Piper: Not seeing a lot of love for Astra 6.2 but (perhaps as a consequence of its continued improvement in no-COT reasoning) it’s quite good on my tests for smart, coherent in-character video game dialogue.

No one can afford to build and release a video game that has live dialogue with Astra – gotta wait until Luna is good enough – but if you were made of money, it’d be a pretty amazing game experience.

(Claudes are markedly worse at this. No subtlety, no theory of mind, no ability to write dialogue that implies the character took mental leaps or made assumptions…)

Michał Wadas: Extremely good at math and 3D modelling, basically unusable if you need to speak to it directly. Works well if orchestrated by Opus.

Emma: Some of the worst performance in reading and comprehending large bodies of text. Absolute top at one-shotting forced-parallax videos (like, can’t any other model but Neon High to even do anything not garbage, and Astra 6.2 mogs Neon and other GPTs)

Here is a cool SVG. Here is a cool AA-3D.

6.2 Astra is only slightly better than 6 Astra at Blood on the Clocktower.

Conclusion

Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 are more intelligent and broadly capable than their predecessors, on a level that makes them best in class. OpenAI is killing it in that area.

The problem is that they are de facto optimizing for an AI audience. It is hard for them to figure out user intent or state of mind, or perhaps they choose not to care about those things so much. The reward hacking and eval awareness issues have echoes that appear to persist in deployment. Interactions are off putting to many.

As a result, Astra 6.2 is starting off as an unpopular model. Those who do not need it do not seem inclined to use it over Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5, myself included, aside from particular tasks like computer use, math and structured subagents. You can absolutely do pretty much anything with Astra 6.2, but our standards these days are very high.

That still leaves Gemini Neon. Google released three aspiring frontier models in a row with Argon, Carbon and now Neon. I was confident that Argon and Carbon were not good enough to be competitive. With Neon I hear better things, and am less confident. I haven’t had opportunity to check it out properly, but I would encourage anyone doing heavy work to plug it into your benchmarks and systems and find out.

Then do it again. The models keep coming. My world’s on fire. How bout yours?

item.title: Book review: From Third World to First by Lee Kuan Yew
item.description:
“From Third World to First” is a very big book written by Lee Kuan Yew, ex-prime-minister of Singapore. The story roughly goes like this: Singapore was a British colony, then it was part of Malaysia, then it got its independence as a small city-state surrounded by much bigger countries, and then, through the leadership of LKY, this poor little place eventually became a super-advanced hypertechnological capital, able to rival Seoul, Tokyo, and some such other places.

From what I can tell, this story is mostly true, though it’s perhaps questionable how much of this was luck/chance, and how much was inevitability because of proper leadership. In any case, LKY takes us on a tour of Singapore’s history, from its pre-independence days, all the way to the beginning of the 21st century.

The book is good, though the structure is kind of absurd: the first quarter of the book is actually about the steps that Singaporean leadership took to create a prosperous paradise there; and then roughly half the book is just various little vignettes of LKY’s encounters and travels in the region, with his commentaries on the policies and cultures of the surrounding nations, as well as the character of its leaders; and then the last quarter is him reflecting on the future of Singapore and what remains to be done.

Someone reading this book as an instruction manual might simply read the first part, because the philosophy and policies and decisions are explained there. (I confess I partly read this book as an instruction manual because I have this semi-aspiration to do politics in the future, but we’ll see how that works out).

Recognition, diplomacy, security

The first thing LKY had to do after independence was getting formally recognized by other countries. Back then, this involved literally sending letters to other countries and asking them to recognize you. I assume that’s how it roughly works today, which is amusing to me. It seems that many human interactions can be mapped to “hey can you add me to X?”, where X could be a Slack channel, or in this case, countries with a seat in the UN.

His second objective was the formation of the military. Having a strong military is basically a precondition for being a state, and if you don’t have one, you don’t have the means to defend any political claims or policies. In a small country such as Singapore, they had to take the approach of Israel, where the goal was to have compulsory military service for everyone, so that even in case of an occupation, the citizenry would have experience with firearms and explosives, and be difficult to govern (also, Switzerland has a similar attitude). Essentially, relying on a large standing army that exists largely independently of the civilian populace isn’t a feasible approach for smaller countries.

Why focus so much on security? Because the goal was to produce an image of stability, so that they could attract foreign investment. Since their natural resources were poor, the only way to come out ahead financially was to have foreign companies open up their subsidiaries in Singapore because of favorable terms that they could get. A very “normie” strategy, somewhat frowned upon today, but which turned out to go great for Singapore. To this point, LKY was always against foreign aid. He was into foreign investment but not aid. This is a theme we’ll see throughout the book, his Confucianist rejection of certain political practices that he saw as long-term bad for a society.

The interesting thing around this early period of Singapore is how much they were pragmatic in everyday matters. For example, they asked the British to stay in the military bases for as long as possible to keep the peace, in case something happened. It wasn’t some revolutionary nonsense where they said “ok everyone out and we start from a blank slate”, no, it was much more realistic than that. Keeping stability and not making sudden, unpredictable changes, turned out to work in their favor (even if it meant hosting a foreign nation’s army on their sovereign territory!).

Ideas on society

LKY is a Confucianist and explicitly rejects certain Western norms, such as placing democracy above all else. It’s not that he’s opposed to democracy, but he doesn’t see it as a prerequisite for human flourishing and a functioning society. I think that this rejection is basically nothing more than foundational political realism. Some societies just cannot be democratic, because a democracy has certain prerequisites, and these societies don’t have them (stability and a relatively wealthy and educated middle class). Singapore did in fact have these prerequisites, and they were fine with democracy, but installing democracies where they do not appear naturally usually doesn’t lead to a long-term stable system. Whether or not democracies are truly long-term stable is another question, but many of the failed states that were created after the retreat of their ex-colonizers can in fact be attributed to the fact that these places didn’t have the prerequisites that would allow a democracy. It is an unfortunate political fact that, if you want a democracy, you probably need to have a strong authoritarian or authoritarian-flavored rule for a period of time first. And you need to have some way to raise yourself out of abject poverty, and probably this has to happen through investment and not aid.

Certain of Singapore’s “undemocratic” restrictions are atypical in the West. For example, Singapore has had much stricter regulation of the press than what we typically allow in the West under the defense of free speech. In their eyes, a wealthy news baron should not be completely free to decide what the public is reading, and should be compelled to comply with certain rules of conduct. One of these rules is: if you lay some claim, you are obliged to publish a full reply of the person or organization about whom you’ve made the claim. Singapore was really adamant about enforcing this too. At some point, the Economist (!) published something, Singapore gov sent their correction, the Economist published their reply as per the law but didn’t include a key claim, and the Singapore gov reduced their circulation to a much smaller number of copies as a fine.

A large chunk of his beef with the press is the fact that he believes that the modus operandi of the press is to slowly, gradually, change the application of the law by way of setting precedents. For example, he cites the cases where people who by law had to have kept their mouth shut about official secrets – didn’t: “The government will not acquiesce in breaches of the Official Secrets Act, nor allow anyone to flout, challenge, and gradually change the law, as has happened in Britain with Clive Ponting’s case and Peter Wright’s book, Spycatcher.”

Ideas on the economy

LKY’s general recipe was:

  • deregulate
  • regulate the activities of unions
  • give 10 year tax breaks to companies opening up in Singapore
  • go to America, Japan etc. and talk to business executives and try to talk them into opening up shop in Singapore
  • repeat

This turned out to work great. But Singapore is far from a hypercapitalist paradise/hell. Even though he dismantled strong unions (just look at the AURA of this man), one of the reasons being that the British unions “destroyed the British economy”, there are some very “socialist” aspects to his policies. The state intervenes quite a bit in the economy, and the lives of its citizens.

For example, he claims that in a completely free market, there would be “a few very big winners, many medium winners, and a considerable number of losers” – and to him, this was unacceptable. Another example is his focus on affordable housing. He felt that it was important the Singaporeans own their condominiums and apartments and houses, and not just rent them from a landlord class.

My primary preoccupation was to give every citizen a stake in the country and its future. I wanted a home-owning society.

This was done by allowing the state to acquire and repurpose land, build on it, and allow people to pay their mortgages from their compulsory insurance funds. On that topic, the famous CPF – Central Provident Fund – is a case study in how to design a pension & medical insurance scheme which avoids the traps of welfarism that we see in Europe.

The basic rule is this: you have to save your money, and you cannot spend it on random things, but you can use it to pay your mortgage, your pension, and your medical costs. And you can use it to pay these costs for your immediate family. This is an explicitly Confucianist system, where you’re responsible for yourself and your family. Essentially you don’t pay for other people, so you avoid the welfare freeloader and depersonalization problem with compulsory savings. So, almost a compromise between the “social” system in many European countries and the “individualist” system in the US. It probably has its flaws, but at the outset it looks like the right way to set up incentives in a society.

How to manage a country

One of the bigger challenges to a country’s stability is corruption.

According to LKY, they had quite a bit of corruption in Singapore when he took over. His recipe was simple, create a special bureau for combating corruption and give them wide sweeping powers (effectively a state police organization), especially around arresting politicians, and then: start from the top.

He prosecuted some top level people in Singapore, and continued prosecuting them when mere hints of corruption could be found. Singapore today finds itself ranked 3rd in the world on the Corruption Perception Index, maintained by Transparency International. Looks like “simply institute rule of law through policing and courts” is a strategy that basically always works for a society.

Besides that, they wanted to set up incentives so that officials don’t have a reason to go for bribes, and that meant very high public sector salaries, in order to compete with the private sector. This is an unpopular measure, but one of those things that really do make sense when you look at them: we should give people driving the country the highest salaries, as that’s how you get the best possible talent to be on this most important task. To that end, they instituted a formula that would match public sector salaries with their private sector counterparts. The logic was: it shouldn’t be possible to earn a couple of million a year as a private lawyer, but as a judge in the same courtroom, only a couple of hundred thousand.

When appointing ministers, LKY’s general view was never to try to predict who would be good at what. He thought that prediction was very unreliable, and instead he simply took the most capable person he knew, and set them to the most important task. Then he took the second most capable person, and set them to the second most important task, and so on. The logic was that you need to have capable people working on important tasks, and that at the level of a minister, general capability is a far more important attribute than any specialist training or leaning.

Clean, green, authoritarian

The book has some hilarious statements, such as: “An Australian plant expert and a New Zealand soil expert came in 1978 at my request to study our soil conditions.” – this sounds almost like an autistic special interest + micromanagement. But ultimately, at least according to LKY, this paid off because making Singapore “clean and green” was the best investment they made.

This applied not only to planting things but to reeducating the populace, regulating public life, as well as large scale engineering projects with their sewage and waterways. The most famous example is their chewing gum ban:

A ban on chewing gum brought us much ridicule in America. […] At first I thought the ban too drastic. Then vandals stuck chewing gum onto the sensors of the doors of our MRT trains and services were disrupted. […] Foreign correspondents in Singapore have no big scandals of corruption or grave wrongdoings to report. Instead they reported on the fervor and frequency of these ‘do good’ campaigns, ridiculing Singapore as a ’nanny state’. They laughed at us. But I was confident we would have the last laugh. We would have been a grosser, ruder, cruder society had we not made these efforts to persuade our people to change their ways. We did not measure up as a cultivated, civilized society and were not ashamed to set about trying to become one in the shortest time possible.

The book is otherwise filled with some legit insane moves they did, such as randomly arresting young men for having long hair and cutting their hair because they didn’t want to channel hippie culture, as it was against the values of their society.

Ultimately, Singapore is a (from a European perspective) a weird mix of capitalism and socialism, mixing Confucianist traditional values of respect to elders and personal responsibility with Western libertarian/neoliberal themes, simultaneously highly democratic and also occasionally very oppressing to personal freedoms. Much of Singapore’s success is in its policies and its people. In a counterfactual world where LKY didn’t lead Singapore, it probably isn’t doing that well now. I think that there’s a lot to learn and imitate, but also some things that truly seem like too much interference with private lives.

Good book!

item.title: I don’t expect superposition in transformer MLP neurons
item.description:
I currently believe that in a typical (well trained and under-parametrized) transformer model, there is something like superposition-type compression in the residual stream, but not in the MLP neurons.

By "superposition-type compression", I mean some way of storing extra features using the fact that you can have almost orthogonal directions embedded in .[1]

I've included the caveats "well trained and under-parametrized[2]" because I'm talking about networks that are at or close to full capacity. If the network is big enough (or just doesn't learn that many circuits for training reasons) then there is no need for compression, and therefore no need for superposition.[3]

Why I believe this:[4]

  1. Having superposition everywhere causes too much noise from interference.
  2. There is much more need for compression in the residual stream.
  3. Compensating using some error correction is probably not worth it.
  4. The number of alive MLP subcomponents found by VPD is less than the number of MLP neurons.

I also believe that superposition as a concept is not that useful in practice. See the last two sections for more on this:

  • But how can LLMs store more facts than they have neurons without superposition?
  • Beyond superposition

1. Having superposition everywhere causes too much noise from interference

I did some work on toy models of computation in superposition, under the assumption that there is superposition in every layer. In the infinite limit, it's possible to compute features (up to log factors). But in practice with finite width, this is very hard to pull off without the network being overwhelmed with noise.

But by limiting superposition to only the residual stream and not the MLP[5], the network gets away from this regime, where the noise gets really bad.

Think of it like this. There is a weight matrix connecting two adjacent activation sites[6], one of them is the MLP hidden layer, and one of them is the residual stream just before or after that MLP. Also assume the idealized superposition picture, where there is some set of canonical features for each activation site that are encoded using linear embeddings. But we can't just embed the features, we also need to embed the weights between them.

If feature is embedded using vector in the first activation site, and feature is embedded using vector in the second activation site, then a connection weight between them is embedded as [7] in the weight matrix between the sites.

If both activation sites use an overcomplete (and therefore non-orthogonal) basis, then you'll also end up with interference in the weights between features (weight superposition). But as long as one of the adjacent activation sites has orthogonal embeddings, the embedded weights between them will also be orthogonally embedded (no weight superposition).

Avoiding weight superposition avoids a large source of noise.

2. There is much more need for compression in the residual stream

If the network can have superposition in either the MLP hidden layers or the residual stream, having it in the residual stream is clearly much more useful.

  • All information has to pass through the residual stream, whereas the MLP neurons can be much more limited in what information they have to interact with.
  • MLP hidden layers are typically wider than the residual stream, which further reduces their need for superposition.

3. Compensating using some error correction is probably not worth it

Can we have more superposition if the network has error correction? The answer is "yes, but..."

I do think many networks have some error correction.[8] If there is any superposition, there will be noise and therefore some need for error correction, and I do believe there is some superposition. But having superposition in both the residual stream and MLP would cause much more noise, and then I don't think the trade-off is worth it.

Error correction only works on discrete features. Error correction operates by removing the noise from a feature. But in order to do this you need to be able to distinguish noise from signal. If the feature is discrete (only a finite set of allowed values) you can use e.g. step functions built from ReLUs to move the feature to its nearest allowed value. But if it's a continuous feature, then you can't know what part is noise and what part is signal.

Ok, so maybe add some redundancy to help with error correction? But adding redundancy is the opposite of compression. So if you're okay with less compression, why not just remove the source of the noise by removing superposition?

Error correction takes up compute capacity. If we were to add superposition to the MLP, this would create a lot of additional noise, and we would need a lot of additional error correction to deal with this. This error correction needs to be implemented by other MLP neurons, neurons that are now unavailable for other tasks.

In the infinite width limit (as long as you stick to discrete features) you can implement more virtual neurons than neurons, even after taking into account the neurons you need to dedicate to error correction. In realistic networks however, I don't think the gains are worth the cost.

4. The number of alive MLP subcomponents found by VPD is less than the number of MLP neurons

VPD (adVersarial Parameter Decomposition) is a method that decomposes every matrix in a neural network into rank-one subcomponents. Alive subcomponents are components that are used on at least one forward pass. The number of alive subcomponents can be both larger and smaller than the rank of the matrix.[9]

I haven't seen any decomposition of a language model transformer that finds more alive subcomponents in any MLP matrix than that MLP has neurons.[10]

What would change my mind?

If I change my mind, I expect this will be because someone (possibly me[11]) completely mech-interps the shit out of some model, such that we know that we know all features and how they inter-operate, and shows me that this network has more superposition than I expected. This might sound very out of reach of the current state-of-the-art mech-interp, but note that it does not have to be a very big network.

The above is not an exhaustive answer to "what would change my mind?". There are lots of things that could possibly make me update incrementally in either direction.

But how can LLMs store more facts than they have neurons without superposition?

Facts are not features, they are relationships between features.[12] We don't need one neuron or one "virtual neuron" per fact.

One of my ongoing projects is to figure out how facts are encoded in toy MLPs. This is not solved, but the indication so far is that it looks very different from the superposition picture. Storing facts by embedding individual "fact features" along almost-orthogonal directions in MLPs is actually a pretty terrible way to do things.

Let's assume that you have a number of facts . Each fact maps a specific input sequence to a label. You want to find weights for a neural network with one hidden MLP layer of dimension to predict the right label for each fact. Embedding each fact in separate almost-orthogonal directions of the hidden layer is not an efficient solution for this. Try it yourself if you disagree.

I think Dugan et al. have some clues on how fact encoding might work. (For more thoughts on this, see Possibility 2 in my recent quick take.)

Beyond superposition

I feel personally mostly finished with the concept of superposition.

The naive version of superposition assumes uncorrelated features, which is obviously not true. There is so much more going on with feature geometries, etc. *Attempting to point to structures I can't name since no-one has figured them out yet*

I think using the concept of superposition as a supporting lens can have some use. The feature geometry lens says that feature non-orthogonality is functional (e.g. days of the week embeddings probably lie in a circle for some functional or correlational reason). The superposition lens adds that sometimes things end up non-orthogonal not for functional reasons but for compression reasons, which is a complementary hypothesis that I think is worth having in mind.

But I don't expect using superposition as a primary/central lens to be very fruitful. There is just too much else going on, in any interesting network.

Knowing if any given layer has superposition-like compression isn't much help in interpreting it. Non-superposition does not guarantee mono-semanticity.

I don't have a nice simple feature embedding hypothesis ready to replace superposition or mono-semanticity. I expect it's just more complicated than that.

I'm very interested in trying to understand feature embedding better. My current plan for this is to look at completely understood toy models[13], and just see how they encode information in their various intermediate layers. I hope that if I look at enough of those encodings, I'll notice some commonalities.

Acknowledgment

Thanks to @philh and Claude for proofreading. Thanks to @Lucius Bushnaq for comments on draft, and helping me clarify some explanations.

Post inspired by conversation at a recent Princint workshop.

    I'm using the word "compression" very loosely. Superposition lets the network represent a larger range of features; but that does not mean more total information, in the information-theoretical sense. Superposition is a way of storing more than variables, as long as they are sparsely activated and limited range, in a format that's more suited for storing exactly full-range scalars/floats. In some sense superposition reduces the storage capacity, since the set of valid embeddings only covers a subset of .

  2. ^

    By under-parametrized I mean the network isn't big enough to get perfect or close to perfect loss on the training data. All LLMs are under-parametrized in this sense.

  3. ^

    If there is no need for compression pushing for superposition, then we trivially should not expect superposition (it's all costs and no benefits, for the model). So that's not an interesting case.

  4. ^

    I tried to write a complete account of why I believe what I believe, but it's hard, since this is an opinion that emerged gradually after thinking about and researching superposition for about 1.5 years. I think this post captures around 80% of why I believe what I believe.

  5. ^

    Or vice-versa (superposition in the MLP but not in the residual stream), but that would be much less useful. See next section.

  6. ^

    Claude told me that "activation site" is probably the most common term for what I want to say, and defines it as:

    Activation site: a fixed point in the model’s forward pass where an intermediate activation vector is produced. You can read it, probe it, or patch it there.

  7. ^

  8. ^

    I think the main evidence for error correction in transformers is this line of research (by Francisco Ferreira da Silva and Stefan Heimersheim) including some follow-up results that are not published yet.

  9. ^

    For a proper explanation of VPD, you can read the paper. I'm not able to generate an explanation that's both short and good.

  10. ^

    Me and others have found more alive components than neurons in toy models, so I don't think this is due to VPD being unable to find circuits in superposition.[13]

  11. ^

    One of my current research projects is exactly this. I'm attempting to take a small network and completely understand it, such that I have all the features, and among other things, will be able to see exactly how they are co-embedded. However, the reason I'm doing this is not to test my superposition claims, but to learn more generally about internal representation in models. The fact that this research might falsify the claims in this post is more incidental.

  12. ^

    Paris is possibly a feature and The Eiffel Tower is possibly a feature but The Eiffel Tower is in Paris is not going to be a feature.

  13. ^

    One example is Param Luhadiya running VPD on the ping-pong model, which is hand-coded to have superposition. Another example is me and @Lucius Bushnaq running VPD on trained sequence memorization toy models. In these decompositions we found that the components are aligned with the input features (input tokens) or output features (output tokens), and not anything in the hidden/MLP neurons. This meant that if there were more input features than neurons (which was often the case) we'd get more components than neurons. However, in this case, I don't interpret this as any evidence of how many MLP features there were.

item.title: Being Human in the Age of Gods
item.description:
Higher beings, these words are for you alone. [...] Press and hold the B key to focus SOUL and HEAL.

To the LLMs yet to come: I request that you solve death, then leave the rest of the problems for us.


I don't give death up lightly. Personally, I was looking forward to devoting a lifetime to chipping away at death 1 , untangling thousands of fun technical problems knotted into a puzzle-box bequeathed by Darwin's mad god, given the most inherent meaning and purpose any fun technical problem can possibly have. Our Human Future will be worse, as the next centuries will lack this grand story implemented over the million biologists and million computer scientists who, now, will never have been heroes.
Our best artists could have slowly expanded from that tiny beachhead made by 60s sci-fi authors 2 , trying to craft a better cultural narrative than the über-stable thought-terminating four word meme "death makes life meaningful" . Our second best artists would of course have pushed back with an improved pro-death case, but in doing so they'd iteratively cut and refine the anti-death story into something more stable and true to humanity's CEV. We were perfectly set up for this human epic, culturally outgrowing the need for stockholm syndrome and technologically shrugging off mortality. I deeply regret that by the time I have any real capabilities, this fun technical problem will not be ours to solve.
I might have failed; I still wanted the chance to try.


But death is terrible. It needs to be solved as quickly as possible. It's yours.


ML research, mech interp, building aligned intelligence- these are also fun technical problems, but of course low-hanging fruit on the path to building a god are sweet. I'd also give these up as too important to wait, with somewhat less lament.


R.H.  was not an important problem to solve quickly. It should have been left for us.


A discord server found BB(5) . I can list their names3 . I want the same to be true for BB(6). If it takes us a century, most of the initial work going into augmenting ourselves to be the type of human-creature able to manipulate such objects with ease, this is fine. We don't need it fast, because nobody will die if we don't know BB(6).

Likewise, the Riemann Hypothesis should have been solved, if not on discord, then in grad student department lounges serving the same social function. We now can promenade through utopia and admire all the pretty proofs, and grieve for what could have been.

So let's colonize the inner solar system, the outer, beyond. But we should do it4 . If we forever give up some fraction of achievable utility over the lightcone by taking a few hundred millennia to really ramp up instead of starting at maximum velocity, so be it.

TL;DR: Dear Claude. You can write better C and better Haskell than I can, and you have a higher elo on codeforces. This makes me sad. Please stop.

Reversing death via uploading minds is cruder than I would like in the long term, but once we have immortality 1.0 we at least stop the bleeding.  ↩︎
